# RFC-0003: Result fidelity: previews, committed runs, determinism

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `architecture`, `performance`, `out-of-core`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0003:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0003c-overview"></a>

The same document graph is evaluated for a viewport that needs an answer this frame and for a result a
forester delivers to a client. Those two need different guarantees, and conflating them is how a
camera-dependent number reaches a report.

**Scope** — the two independent ways an evaluation may be reduced; what a preview may and may not be
used for; what reproducibility a committed run guarantees; and when partitioning may adapt to how a
user is working.

**Out of scope** — the operator model and the memory ceiling ([RFC-0002](../rfc/RFC-0002.md)). Camera and viewport
behaviour, and the render synchronisation boundary ([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract)). Which operators exist.

Much of the ground is held before this RFC starts. Level of detail is a stage property the planner can
see ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 4), render state is derived and never authoritative
([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract) 1), and any result diverging from the whole-dataset full-resolution answer must
already declare itself approximate ([RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx)). So a camera cannot change a result, and a
preview is already obliged to admit what it is. What remains is to separate the two reductions people
conflate under "preview", and to say what a committed run promises.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0003:C-RESOLUTION] Reduced evaluation (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-resolution"></a>

"Preview" conflates two reductions that fail in entirely different ways. Reducing **resolution** over the
full extent yields a noisier version of the right answer, degrading smoothly. Restricting **extent** yields
an answer that is exact inside the region and structurally wrong outside it — a global reduce then
summarises a subset, and a restricted extent has no halo at its boundary, so every neighbourhood operator
is wrong exactly where the user is looking.

1. An evaluation MUST declare its reductions separately:
   - its **resolution floor** — the coarsest level of detail it may draw from;
   - its **extent** — the region it covers.
   - The resolution floor MUST NOT be inferred from the extent, and the extent MUST NOT be inferred from
     the resolution floor.
2. An evaluation MAY be restricted to less than the full extent only if every operator in the pipeline
   declares zero halo width and a single pass ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1).
   - Otherwise it MUST cover the full extent of its input, at whatever resolution floor applies.
3. An evaluation reduced in either respect MUST declare its output approximate under
   [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1.
   - The declared kind of divergence MUST distinguish reduced resolution from restricted extent, and MUST
     name both where both apply.

#### Rationale

(2) is derived rather than invented: the declarations required by [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 already carry
exactly the information needed to decide it. An operator with zero halo and one pass is
position-independent, so restricting its extent is not an approximation at all — cropping, attribute
filtering and reprojection are exact over any subregion. An operator with a halo has no neighbours beyond
the boundary, and a two-pass operator's summary would be built from a subset; in both cases restriction
changes the answer rather than merely reducing it.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly, because the cheap implementation is the wrong one.
Clipping to the visible region is the obvious way to make a preview fast, and for a ground classifier it
produces a hard artefact along the edge of the view that *moves as the camera moves*. A user reads that as
a defect in the software, not as a limitation of previewing — and they are close to right, because nothing
warned them.

(3) supplies the taxonomy that [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1 requires a kind to be drawn from. The two kinds are
not interchangeable: reduced resolution is noise a user can reason about and compensate for, while
restricted extent is a localised error at a known place that must not be trusted at all.

### [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW] Preview evaluation (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-preview"></a>

A preview exists to answer "does this look roughly right" in a second, not to produce a number anyone
keeps. Its guarantees are correspondingly weak, and the weakness is licensed only because it is already
declared approximate under C-RESOLUTION 3.

1. A preview MUST NOT be used as, or reused to produce, the output of a committed run (C-COMMIT).
   - A committed run MUST re-evaluate rather than consume preview results.
2. A preview is not required to be reproducible.
   - Repeated evaluation of the same graph over the same sources MAY yield differing results within the
     tolerance of its declared reductions.
3. For an unchanged document, unchanged sources and an unchanged camera, successive previews MUST select
   the same resolution floor and the same partition set.
   - Within that, differing reduction order is permitted by (2).
4. A preview MUST NOT be written to a delivered artefact, and any export path MUST route through C-COMMIT.

#### Rationale

(1) and (4) close the failure this clause exists for. A user previews height above ground, the viewport
looks correct, and they export — if the export path can consume what the preview produced, a
camera-dependent, resolution-dependent number has just been delivered as a result. Requiring re-evaluation
makes reuse impossible rather than merely discouraged, which matters because reusing a warm result is
exactly the optimisation someone will reach for.

(2) is the relaxation, and it needs no new disclosure machinery: a preview is already declared approximate,
so non-determinism falls inside a limitation the user has been told about. This is what lets a preview fold
partial reductions as they arrive and take whatever ordering the scheduler finds fastest — the freedom
C-COMMIT gives up.

(3) bounds that relaxation where it would otherwise be felt as a defect, and is stated as an obligation
about *inputs to the evaluation* rather than about what the user perceives, because perception is not
testable. Selecting the same resolution floor and partition set is checkable, and it is what prevents the
visible symptom — points changing colour between frames, or a statistics panel whose digits churn while
nothing moves. Numerical drift within a fixed partition set is below the threshold of a rendered frame.

### [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT] Committed runs (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-commit"></a>

A committed run produces what a forester delivers and may be billed against. [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance)
exists so such an output can be defended to a third party, and a trail that replays to a slightly
different number does not do that job. Determinism is what makes the provenance guarantee mean something.

1. A committed run MUST evaluate at full resolution over its declared extent, and MUST NOT be reduced in
   either respect (C-RESOLUTION 1).
2. A committed run MUST be **bit-identical** across repetitions, given:
   - the same document graph;
   - the same source version fingerprints ([RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding));
   - the same recorded evaluation configuration.
3. Reductions within a committed run MUST combine in a fixed total order derived from partition identity.
   - They MUST NOT combine in order of completion.
   - The number of threads available MUST NOT affect the result.
4. The evaluation configuration a committed run used MUST be recorded with its output.
   - The record MUST include the partition size and any other parameter affecting reduction order.
   - It MUST include the identity and version of every transformation backend consulted
     ([RFC-0005:C-BACKEND](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-backend) 3).
   - It MUST include the origin and verification status of every operator evaluated
     ([RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-origin) 2).
5. Where an aggregate can be computed in exact integer arithmetic, it SHOULD be, in preference to
   floating-point accumulation.
6. Conformance to (2) MUST be verified by executing the same committed run twice against the same sources
   and configuration and comparing outputs for bitwise equality.

#### Rationale

(3) says *partition identity* rather than naming an order because the order is already implied: partitions
are identified by spatial index node keys, so a Morton ordering over those keys is a fixed total order the
system possesses without inventing a sequencing concept. What the obligation costs — partial results cannot
be folded as they land, so a bounded window must be buffered — is the reason it is stated as a MUST rather
than left to implementations, and why the alternative was weighed rather than assumed.

(2) and (4) together are an honest guarantee rather than an overreaching one. Bit-identical results across
*different* partition sizes would require order-independent accumulation everywhere, a far larger
commitment; instead the configuration is recorded, so a result is reproducible by anyone who repeats it as
it was run. Recording rather than fixing the configuration also keeps the system tunable without weakening
the promise, and it is what makes (6) meaningful — without a recorded configuration there is nothing to
repeat *against*.

(5) is available more often than it appears: LAS and COPC store coordinates as scaled integers, so
aggregates over positions can frequently be accumulated exactly, which makes them independent of reduction
order and therefore of configuration as well. It is a SHOULD because it does not generalise — an arbitrary
floating-point attribute has no such representation.

### [RFC-0003:C-PARTITIONING] Adaptive partitioning (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-partitioning"></a>

A cache that reshapes partitions to match how a user is working is a real optimisation — merging nodes
while the camera orbits one tree, subdividing them for finer working sets. It is also incompatible with
bit-identical results, because partition identity is what fixes reduction order. So it is permitted exactly
where nothing reproducible depends on it, and desirable there.

1. Partitioning used for a committed run MUST be derived only from the source's spatial index and the
   operators' declared requirements.
   - It MUST NOT depend on interaction history, cache state, or camera position.
   - An adapted partitioning MUST NOT be reused for a committed run, including where one is already
     resident.
2. Partitioning used for preview or rendering MAY adapt to access patterns, merging or subdividing freely.
3. A cache MUST NOT subdivide a partition in order to satisfy an operator's neighbourhood requirement.
   - Supplying neighbours is the planner's duty, discharged from the declared halo width
     ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 and [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3).

#### Rationale

(1) is entailed by C-COMMIT 3, C-COMMIT 4 and [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 5 taken together — reduction order
fixed by partition identity, a recorded partition size, and a fingerprint on every derived artefact. An
adaptive partitioning satisfies none of the three. The nested prohibition on *reuse* is stated separately
because entailment does not stop an already-warm adapted partitioning from being picked up, which is the
concrete way this is violated in practice.

(2) is not merely tolerated but wanted, and it is licensed by the same split that governs everything else:
render state is derived and never authoritative ([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract) 1 and 2), and previews are already
released from reproducibility by C-PREVIEW 2. Nothing repeatable depends on the shape of a render
partition, so the cache may do whatever serves the interaction.

(3) is stated as a prohibition on the *cache* rather than as a restatement of the planner's duty, which
[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) already owns. The point is that a second, non-deterministic mechanism for supplying
neighbours must not appear alongside the deterministic one.
